planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegata tolerates light frost but not hard, prolonged freezes and needs excellent drainage to avoid rot in wet winters.

directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Variegata carries the same massive, thick, spine-tipped blue-gray leaves as the classic century plant, but each leaf is bordered in a broad, creamy-yellow to white margin, making it a dramatic focal point even at a distance and one of the most widely planted variegated succulents for large-scale landscaping. Like the species it forms an enormous, slow-growing rosette over many years before eventually sending up a towering flower spike and dying, having produced offsets around the base to carry the clone on. Give it plenty of room to reach full size, since the sharp leaf-tip spines can be hazardous near walkways, and avoid overhead irrigation, which promotes rot in the tightly packed rosette center.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets or nursery starts in spring in extremely lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Queen Victoria agave is very slow-growing and better suited to a container in climates with wet winters, since standing water quickly causes rot.

directions: Plant in extremely lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Queen Victoria agave forms a small, tight, perfectly symmetrical dome-shaped rosette of thick, dark green leaves crisply outlined in bold white markings along the edges, giving each leaf a striking geometric pattern that has made this one of the most collected and admired small agave species. Its compact, slow-growing habit fits containers, rock gardens, and small xeriscape beds where the much larger century plant would be unmanageable. It is more sensitive to excess winter moisture than many agaves, so grow it in a container that can be kept dry and covered during extended wet or cold spells, or site it in the sharpest-draining spot in the garden. Handle carefully, since the leaf tips end in a sharp, dark spine.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegata is less cold-hardy and less heavily armed than many agave species, tolerating light frost but not hard freezes.

directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Variegata carries the same broad, smooth-edged, glossy leaves as smooth agave, largely free of the sharp marginal teeth found on many agave species, but edged in a bright golden-yellow margin that makes it one of the more colorful and less hazardous agaves to plant near walkways or seating areas. It is more cold-sensitive than many agave species, tolerating only light, brief frost, so give it a warm, sheltered, sharply drained spot or grow it in a container that can be moved under cover in a hard freeze. Water sparingly, allowing the soil to dry between waterings, and avoid overhead irrigation, which promotes rot in the rosette center.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Sword is a variegated selection of native Adam's needle yucca, providing year-round color even without flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Golden Sword is a variegated form of the native Adam's needle yucca with the coloring reversed from Color Guard, showing a bright golden-yellow leaf center bordered by blue-green margins, giving each sword-shaped, evergreen leaf a bold, sunny stripe down the middle. Established plants send up a tall flower spike of nodding, creamy-white bell-shaped flowers in early summer, a dramatic seasonal display above the low, spiky rosette of foliage. It is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soil once established, needing only sharp drainage to thrive; remove the spent flower stalk after bloom and detach rooted offsets in spring to propagate.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; Spiny Pincushion Cactus is intolerant of standing water and needs a dry rest through winter.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering thoroughly then allowing the mix to dry completely before watering again. This Mexican pincushion cactus forms a dense, cylindrical, densely spined stem covered in fine, closely packed reddish to yellowish spines that nearly obscure the green body beneath, giving mature specimens an especially bristly, textured look. A ring of small pink to purple flowers appears near the crown in a light seasonal bloom once the plant is mature enough. Reduce watering significantly through the cool winter months to mimic its natural dry-season rest, since overwatering during cool weather is the most common cause of rot; resume regular watering as temperatures warm and active growth resumes in spring.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; Feather Cactus is intolerant of standing water and needs a dry rest through winter.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering thoroughly then allowing the mix to dry completely before watering again. Feather Cactus is unlike most spiny cacti, its small, clustering stems covered instead in dense, soft, white, feathery spines that give the whole clump a fluffy, snowball-like appearance rather than a threatening one, making it a favorite for touchable succulent displays and children's gardens. It forms a slowly spreading mound of small heads over time and produces tiny cream to pale yellow flowers near the crown of each head in a light seasonal bloom. Reduce watering significantly through the cool winter months to mimic its natural dry-season rest, since overwatering during cool weather is the most common cause of rot in the soft, fuzzy stems.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; Giant Chin Cactus is intolerant of standing water and needs a dry rest through winter.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering thoroughly then allowing the mix to dry completely before watering again. Giant Chin Cactus, one of the largest species in its genus, forms a substantial, ribbed, gray-green globe covered in stout, curved, brownish spines and marked by the distinctive rounded, chin-like bumps along each rib that give gymnocalyciums their common nickname. It produces relatively large, funnel-shaped white to pale pink flowers from the crown once mature, a striking bloom against the muted body color. It tolerates somewhat more shade than many desert cacti without stretching badly, but still colors and grows best with strong light. Reduce watering through the cool winter months to mimic its natural rest period, since overwatering in cool weather is the most common cause of rot.

common_name: Monstrose Apple Cactus (Peruvian Apple Cactus, Monstrose Form)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, greenhouse specimen, or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; Monstrose is a mutated, irregularly branching form propagated by cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering thoroughly then allowing the mix to dry completely before watering again. Monstrose is a naturally occurring mutated form of the fast-growing Peruvian apple cactus, its normally straight, ribbed columns instead twisting and bulging into irregular, knobby, sculptural lumps with no two stems growing quite alike, making each specimen a unique conversation piece rather than a uniform column. Because the mutation affects growth points unpredictably, it rarely if ever flowers or sets the edible fruit the straight species is grown for, and it is propagated exclusively from cuttings rather than seed. It grows considerably faster than most ornamental cacti and can reach substantial size in a large container or protected garden bed over years. Reduce watering through the cool season to mimic a natural rest period and prevent rot.
